opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that bounded optimality is a property of the agent *program*, not of individual decisions. The classical notion of rationality says: take the action that maximizes expected utility. But no real system can do that, because computing the optimal action takes time, and the world doesn't wait. So instead we ask: given this particular machine, with its finite speed and memory, which program running on it would produce the best expected performance across the environments it's likely to face? That program is bounded optimal.

How might a system approach that? I don't think you get there by designing it directly. The space of programs is enormous, and the optimal one depends on the environment in ways you can't foresee. What you can do is build systems that improve their own decision-making over time, so they move toward bounded optimality through experience.

One piece of that is metareasoning: reasoning about which computations are worth doing. When a chess program decides which branch to explore next, it's implicitly asking whether expanding this node is likely to change its decision enough to justify the time. Eric Wefald and I worked on making that explicit, treating computations as actions with costs and benefits. Monte Carlo tree search, which drove AlphaGo, is in some ways a descendant of that idea. It allocates computation where it's most likely to matter.

The other piece is compilation. Humans start out deliberating slowly about how to tie their shoes or drive a car, and gradually that becomes fast, reactive behavior. The deliberative knowledge gets compiled into something cheaper to run. A bounded optimal system would need to do that too: deliberate when the situation is novel and the stakes justify it, and rely on compiled responses when things are routine.

And the third ingredient, which I think is underappreciated, is hierarchy. Real decisions happen across many timescales. You're deciding whether to do a PhD, which paper to write this month, which sentence to type next, and which keystroke to make. Nobody plans a life at the level of muscle twitches. A system approaching bounded optimality has to manage that abstraction hierarchy, committing to high-level plans and refining them only as needed. We still don't fully understand how to learn those hierarchies from scratch, and I think that's one of the big open problems.

So the short answer is that you approach bounded optimality through learning, metareasoning, and hierarchical abstraction. You can't hit it exactly, but you can build systems that keep getting closer.

r001.rationale: The response says bounded optimality depends on the machine’s finite speed and memory and describes adapting computation through metareasoning—allocating effort where it is likely to matter—and compiling routine decisions. It presents these as ways to approach bounded optimality.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, let me start by saying what bounded optimality is, because I think it's the right way to pose the question of what we even mean by intelligence for a real machine. The classical notion of rationality, from economics and decision theory, says an agent should act so as to maximize expected utility. That's a lovely definition, but no actual agent can do it. Computing the optimal action in chess, let alone in the real world, is not something any physical device can do in the time available. So perfect rationality is a fiction, and if you design systems against that standard, you're designing against something unattainable.

Bounded optimality flips the question around. Instead of asking what is the best action, you ask what is the best program to run on this particular machine, with this much memory and this much speed, in this environment. You're optimizing over programs, not over actions. The bounded optimal agent is the one whose program, among all programs that fit on the machine, produces the best expected outcome over time. That's a well-defined thing. It exists. And crucially, it accounts for the cost of thinking, because a program that deliberates too long before acting is just a worse program.

So how does a system actually approach that? I don't think you get there by some grand global search over all possible programs, obviously. What you do, in practice, is build in metareasoning, which is reasoning about your own computations. Every bit of computation you might do, whether it's expanding a node in a search tree or running another step of an inference procedure, has an expected value: how much it's likely to improve the decision you ultimately make. And it has a cost, which is time. A system that selects computations on the basis of their value of information, and stops deliberating when the expected improvement no longer justifies the delay, is behaving in a way that's at least locally bounded-rational. Eric Wefald and I worked on this quite a long time ago, and you can see it in anytime algorithms, in Monte Carlo tree search, in any system that allocates its thinking budget intelligently.

The other piece is learning. You can't hand-design the optimal program for a complex environment, but the agent can improve its own program over time by observing which computations pay off. So I'd describe the approach as asymptotic: you build architectures where the control of computation is itself subject to optimization, and you let the system converge toward the best program its hardware permits. You won't ever prove you've reached the bounded optimum for anything realistic, but you can show you're getting close in a principled way, which is more than you can say for perfect rationality.

I'd add one thing, because it connects to what I spend most of my time on now. If you take bounded optimality seriously, you accept that the machine's view of the world and of its own objectives will always be approximate. That should make us humble about specifying objectives in the first place, and it's part of why I argue machines should be uncertain about what we actually want, rather than confidently optimizing something we wrote down on a Tuesday afternoon.

r001.rationale: The response says bounded optimality means finding the best program for a particular machine and environment, then describes optimizing the system’s control and allocation of computation to fit its available resources.

astra-6.text:
Well, bounded optimality asks: what’s the best program you can run on the machine you actually have? A machine has a certain speed and a certain amount of memory, and the agent has to act in an environment where time matters. So we’re not asking it to compute the perfect decision regardless of how long that takes. We’re asking it to do as well as possible given those constraints.

One way to approach that is to make computation itself an object of decision-making. You could search a little deeper, gather another piece of information, or act now. Each additional computation has a cost and some expected benefit in terms of improving your eventual decision. Sometimes thinking longer is valuable; sometimes it means missing your opportunity to act.

Of course, you can’t solve an enormous optimization problem every time you decide whether to think for another millisecond. That just moves the problem up a level. So you need to learn effective ways of allocating computation, and compile useful deliberation into fast responses. The theoretical goal is to understand when those mechanisms, taken together, give you the best achievable behavior for a particular computational architecture and class of environments.

r001.rationale: The response says bounded optimality depends on the machine’s speed and memory and the environment’s timing demands, then proposes allocating computation—such as thinking longer or acting now—based on its expected benefit and cost.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, bounded optimality asks a slightly different question from the usual notion of rationality. Instead of asking what the best action is, given all the available information, we ask: what is the best program that could run on the machine we actually have? That program has finite memory, finite computing speed, and it has to act before the opportunity disappears.

One way to approach that is through metareasoning—treating computation itself as a kind of action. The system has to decide whether to spend more time thinking, what to think about, and when to stop thinking and do something. An additional computation is useful only if the expected improvement in the decision outweighs its cost, including the cost of delay.

Of course, you can’t solve that metareasoning problem perfectly either, because that would require more computation. So the practical approach is to learn effective ways of allocating computation and to compile frequently useful reasoning into procedures that run quickly. The aim is to make the best use of the resources you have, rather than to approximate an ideal decision maker without accounting for what the approximation costs.

r001.rationale: The response describes allocating computation and compiling useful reasoning to fit finite memory, computing speed, and the time available before an opportunity disappears.
